_status: PUBLISHED — this file is on the Verify screen. official_finding is researched prose; udgam_result is regenerated from the bundle by scripts/scaffold_verification.py (never by hand); assessment is the verdict on our own result — for the six live cases it was drafted 14 Sept under Master D43 and is Akshat's to edit and own. Re-run --publish after any edit.

official_finding.summary: The NTSB determined the probable cause of the San Pedro Bay Pipeline rupture was the proximity of established anchorage positions to the pipeline: on 25 January 2021 a strong cold front drove the containerships MSC DANIT and Beijing to drag anchor, and their anchors struck, displaced (~105 ft) and damaged the pipeline. Undetected, fatigue cracks grew until the pipeline leaked ~9 months later, on 1 October 2021. The volume released was worsened by Beta Offshore's insufficient controller training and failure to shut in the line promptly.

responsible_parties.name: MSC DANIT
responsible_parties.role: anchor strike NTSB names as the initiating event

responsible_parties.name: Beijing
responsible_parties.role: second containership that dragged anchor and contacted the pipeline in the same 25 Jan 2021 storm

responsible_parties.name: Amplify Energy Corp. / Beta Offshore
responsible_parties.role: pipeline operator; delayed shutdown increased the volume released

official_finding.source_name: NTSB Marine Investigation Report MIR-24-01, 'Anchor Strike of Underwater Pipeline and Eventual Crude Oil Release'
official_finding.caveat: The anchor strikes preceded the oil release by ~8-9 months. No vessel was transiting or the proximate source at detection time (2 Oct 2021). The source at detection time is fixed infrastructure — the pipeline itself. MIR-24-01's casualty fact table gives the location as 33°34.20' N, 118°7.26' W, 4.75 nm off Huntington Beach. The ~33.66 N figure that circulated earlier was not the NTSB coordinate.

udgam_result.origin_summary: Origin cloud centred at 33.5945° N, 118.0519° W; half the ensemble lands within 1.35 km and nine in ten within 2.46 km. Release window 2021-10-01T17:41:51Z to 2021-10-01T19:58:21Z (convergence). Stage 3 funnel 106 → 75 → 5 → 0. Abstained: the top two vessels score within a few percent of each other and cannot be separated on this evidence

assessment.explanation: Partial in both directions, and written down in advance (D38). NTSB concluded that no transiting vessel was the proximate source in October 2021: the source was the pipeline itself, cracked eight months earlier by two dragging anchors. UDGAM agreed with the half it could reach — 106 vessels in the box, 75 in the window, 5 plausible, then an abstention rather than a name, because the top two scored 0.73 and 0.73 and could not be separated on this evidence. Naming either would have been wrong, and the system declined. It did not reach the other half. meta.json declares the San Pedro Bay Pipeline at NTSB's casualty coordinate, and the infrastructure module scored it about 0.006, far below the 0.25 floor, because our reconstructed origin peak sits 6.74 km from that coordinate with an r90 of 2.46 km and a grid probability of 0.0000 there. The origin is a confident cloud in the wrong place, and the precision is real while the accuracy is not. MSC DANIT and Beijing appear in neither our release-window nor our scene-time extract, which is correct: they were not in these waters at detection time, and no system could name them from this scene alone.
assessment.what_would_have_helped: An origin that reached the pipeline. 6.74 km of displacement with an r90 of 2.46 km is a precision the result does not earn, and the likeliest cause is the current field: this is a nearshore case with a 0.38 wind share, where HYCOM's 0.08° cells and the unresolved tidal component matter most. A higher-resolution nearshore current field, or assimilating the observed slick shape into the rewind rather than only seeding it, is what closes that gap. Second, a chronic-versus-acute classifier: the evidence for a fixed source was on the screen — a slick anchored in a platform field, no vessel able to explain it — and the system had no way to say 'this looks like infrastructure' out loud, which is what NTSB found.
